subject: Biology
title: Brain Imaging Technology
description: A fast breakdown of Brain Imaging Technology for builders.

hook.text: A century ago, the only way to study the brain was to wait for someone to die and examine it.

buildup.text: MRI scans reveal brain structure in detail. fMRI shows which areas are active during tasks.

discovery.text: EEG measures electrical waves from the scalp, tracking brain activity in real time.

twist.text: PET scans use radioactive tracers to watch glucose metabolism—showing which brain areas work hardest.

climax.text: Brain imaging has transformed neuroscience, revealing how we think, feel, and decide.

punchline.text: Now we can watch the brain think—live.

quiz.question: What does fMRI measure?
options: Which brain areas are active during tasks

details.summary: Brain imaging technologies like MRI, fMRI, PET, and EEG allow scientists to visualize brain structure and activity without surgery. Each technique offers different tradeoffs between spatial resolution, temporal resolution, and invasiveness.
details.whyItMatters: Brain imaging revolutionized neuroscience by letting researchers watch the living brain at work. It has transformed diagnosis of neurological conditions and our understanding of how different brain regions contribute to thought and behavior.
takeaways: MRI shows detailed brain structure; fMRI shows activity via blood flow
EEG captures electrical activity in real time but with poor spatial detail
PET scans track radioactive tracers to map metabolic brain activity

faq.question: What is the difference between MRI and fMRI?
faq.answer: MRI produces detailed structural images of brain anatomy. fMRI measures changes in blood oxygenation as a proxy for neural activity, showing which brain regions are active during specific tasks. Structure versus function.

faq.question: Can brain scans read your thoughts?
faq.answer: Not in the science-fiction sense. Brain scans can identify broad patterns associated with categories of thought, like viewing faces versus houses. But decoding specific thoughts, intentions, or memories remains far beyond current technology.
